Three-lined tongue sole (Cynoglossus abbreviatus) attains a maximum total length of 37.9 centimeters [Li = 37.9 centimeters], making it a moderately sized flatfish within its genus along the continental shelf of the western Pacific. Field surveys have documented that the size at which individuals first undergo gonadal activation, corresponding to the total length at puberty, is 19 centimeters [Lp = 19 centimeters], a threshold that marks the transition from the juvenile growth phase to the onset of reproductive competence. This value was derived from macroscopic examination of gonadal condition across a size-stratified sample, revealing that approximately half of all individuals examined at this length exhibited developing ovaries or testes. The relatively modest size at maturation suggests that this species allocates a substantial portion of its early life to somatic expansion before diverting resources toward gamete production. Comparisons with congeneric species such as Cynoglossus semilaevis indicate a broadly similar pattern, although the absolute length at maturation varies with local environmental conditions and density-dependent factors. Such life-history traits are consistent with an iteroparous reproductive strategy common among pleuronectiform fishes inhabiting soft-bottom continental shelf habitats.

Gravid females of the three-lined tongue sole exhibit a gonadosomatic index (GSI) of 7% [GSI = 7%] during the spawning season at a water temperature of 27.5 °C [T = 27.5 °C]. This measure of reproductive allocation, which is comparatively modest among flatfishes, suggests that females partition their annual energy budget conservatively, producing a relatively small ovarian mass relative to body weight. The field measurements were obtained from individuals captured during the peak spawning period in the East China Sea, where surface temperatures regularly approach this thermal regime. The ultimate female wet weight recorded for this population reaches 291 grams [Wwi = 291 grams], representing the asymptotic body mass that fully mature females achieve under favorable foraging conditions. This value aligns well with length-weight relationships derived from extensive trawl survey data, which indicate that females continue to increase in mass gradually even after reaching reproductive maturity. The combination of a low gonado-somatic index and a relatively large asymptotic mass implies a life-history strategy emphasizing somatic persistence and gradual growth rather than a single massive reproductive bout.

At the onset of reproductive maturity, the wet weight at puberty for female three-lined tongue sole is 32.6 grams [Wwp = 32.6 grams], a body mass that corresponds to the 19-centimeter length threshold described earlier. The length-weight scaling exponent derived from population samples confirms that this mass represents a critical energetic threshold that must be reached before vitellogenesis can commence. In contrast, the neonates of this species enter the world at a remarkably small size, with an estimated wet weight at birth of 0.000092 grams [Wwb = 0.000092 grams], a value approximated from the egg diameter of related species within the genus. This minuscule initial mass is characteristic of marine teleosts that produce numerous small pelagic eggs, a strategy that maximizes fecundity at the expense of per-offspring investment. The newly hatched yolk-sac larvae rely entirely on endogenous yolk reserves during the first days post-eclosion, facing high mortality rates until they successfully initiate exogenous feeding. Such extreme altriciality at birth imposes strong selective pressure for rapid early growth and efficient yolk utilization under the warm, productive conditions of the continental shelf.

Hatching of Cynoglossus abbreviatus occurs after an incubation period of 2.9 days [ab = 2.9 days] when eggs are maintained at 27.5 °C [T = 27.5 °C], a brief developmental window typical of small pelagic teleost eggs spawned in warm waters. The rapid embryonic development, driven by elevated metabolic rates at this temperature, means that the yolk-sac larva emerges before substantial differentiation of the digestive tract has occurred, leaving the larva in an endotrophic state for the first several days of life. Data from laboratory rearing trials indicate that the timing of chorion rupture is tightly linked to thermal conditions, with slight deviations in incubation temperature producing measurable shifts in hatching synchrony. Once emerged, the prolarvae measure only a few millimeters in length and possess a prominent yolk sac that sustains them until the mouth opens and the retina differentiates sufficiently for prey detection. The short ab value for this species is broadly consistent with that reported for other warm-water cynoglossids, reflecting the general acceleration of embryonic ontogeny at elevated temperatures. Following hatching, the lecithotrophic phase gives way to first exogenous feeding within a matter of additional days.

The maximum documented lifespan for the three-lined tongue sole, recorded under stable thermal conditions in captivity, is approximately 2190 days [am = approximately 2190 days], which corresponds to roughly six years of life at a water temperature of 27.5 °C [T = 27.5 °C]. This longevity value places the species among the shorter-lived members of the Cynoglossidae, consistent with its relatively small maximum size and early maturation schedule. Wild-caught individuals rarely exceed four to five years of age based on otolith increment analysis, suggesting that natural mortality rates are elevated in the variable conditions of the continental shelf, where trawling pressure and predation by larger demersal fishes take a substantial toll. The captive lifespan data, gathered from individuals maintained in flow-through seawater systems, likely represent the upper physiological boundary of the species, absent the extrinsic mortality factors encountered in the field. The observed life span, coupled with the modest gonadal investment and the relatively early age at puberty, suggests a life-history strategy that balances current reproduction against the probability of surviving to future breeding seasons, a classic iteroparous trade-off. Juveniles settling in nursery grounds along the continental shelf encounter a heterogeneous environment shaped by seasonal upwelling and variable benthic prey availability, factors that influence both growth rate and the onset of sexual maturation. This species' life history, marked by a short incubation period and a relatively low gonado-somatic index, reflects adaptations common among flatfishes occupying highly productive yet unpredictable coastal ecosystems.
